restaurant.name: Salateen Restaurant
restaurant.shortDescription: A Swabi institution for charcoal BBQ, hand-pressed Chapli Kabab and Kabuli Pulao served on trays built for ten.
restaurant.longDescription: Salateen Restaurant Swabi stands on Jhangira Road in Mal Lar, where the Grand Trunk traffic slows and the smell of charcoal reaches the road before the signboard does. The kitchen is unapologetically Pakhtun: mutton karahi finished in copper, seekh kabab turned by hand over open coals, and Kabuli Pulao steamed in a degh large enough to feed a wedding. Portions are famously generous. The full platter comfortably seats ten around a single tray, which is why families drive in from Mardan and Nowshera for graduations, walimas and plain Friday lunches. Three halls, a partitioned family wing with full purdah, and a lawn beside the grill pits mean the room adapts to the occasion rather than the other way round. Everything is halal, everything is cooked to order, and the green tea never stops arriving.

menu.name: Beef Seekh Kabab
menu.shortDescription: Hand-rolled minced beef, charred over coals, four to a plate.
menu.description: Minced beef worked with green chilli, coriander and roasted cumin, packed onto flat iron skewers and turned over charcoal until the outside blisters and the inside stays loose. Served with sliced onion, lemon and the house mint chutney. This is the item most reviewers name first, and the kitchen sends out several hundred skewers on a Friday night.
menu.seoTitle: Beef Seekh Kabab | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Hand-rolled minced beef, charred over coals, four to a plate.

menu.name: Chicken Tikka Boti
menu.shortDescription: Yoghurt-and-red-chilli marinade, twelve hours, then coals.
menu.description: Boneless thigh cut into thumb-sized pieces and left overnight in yoghurt, red chilli, garlic and mustard oil. Grilled fast so the edges catch and the centre stays wet. Comes with naan, salad and chutney.
menu.seoTitle: Chicken Tikka Boti | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Yoghurt-and-red-chilli marinade, twelve hours, then coals.

menu.name: Charcoal Mutton Chops
menu.shortDescription: Rib chops, dry-rubbed, finished directly on the coals.
menu.description: Rib chops rubbed with black pepper, ajwain and salt, seared over the hottest part of the grill and rested. No sauce, nothing to hide behind. Six chops to a portion.
menu.seoTitle: Charcoal Mutton Chops | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Rib chops, dry-rubbed, finished directly on the coals.

menu.name: Batair Roast (Quail)
menu.shortDescription: Whole quail, split and grilled. The adventurous order.
menu.description: Two whole quail, butterflied, marinated in ginger and white pepper and grilled whole. Reviewers call it the unexpected highlight of the menu. Eat it with your hands.
menu.seoTitle: Batair Roast (Quail) | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Whole quail, split and grilled. The adventurous order.

menu.name: River Fish Fry
menu.shortDescription: Besan-crusted river fish, fried in the open karahi.
menu.description: Whole river fish scored, coated in a spiced gram-flour batter and lowered into the wide open karahi over a wood fire. Crisp outside, flaking inside. Winter is the season for it.
menu.seoTitle: River Fish Fry | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Besan-crusted river fish, fried in the open karahi.

menu.name: The Grand Platter
menu.shortDescription: One tray, ten hands. Mutton, chicken, seekh and Kabuli rice.
menu.description: The dish Salateen is known for beyond Swabi. A single steel tray carrying Kabuli Pulao, mutton roash, chicken tikka, beef seekh, chapli kabab and salad, sent out to the table whole. Reviewers routinely report feeding ten people from one platter for around six thousand rupees. Order it forty minutes ahead if you can.
menu.seoTitle: The Grand Platter | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: One tray, ten hands. Mutton, chicken, seekh and Kabuli rice.

menu.name: Chapli Kabab
menu.shortDescription: Coarse beef, pomegranate seed and tomato, pressed flat.
menu.description: The Peshawari benchmark. Coarse-minced beef bound with egg and cornmeal, studded with anardana and green chilli, pressed into wide discs and shallow-fried in beef fat with a tomato slice set into the top. Ordered by weight, exactly as the menu card lists it.
menu.seoTitle: Chapli Kabab | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Coarse beef, pomegranate seed and tomato, pressed flat.

menu.name: Chicken Chapli Kabab
menu.shortDescription: The same method, lighter mince, for those who prefer chicken.
menu.description: Minced chicken thigh treated exactly like the beef version, with a little extra coriander to carry the flavour. Popular with children and with the family hall.
menu.seoTitle: Chicken Chapli Kabab | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: The same method, lighter mince, for those who prefer chicken.

menu.name: Mutton Karahi
menu.shortDescription: Tomato, ginger and green chilli. Nothing else in the pan.
menu.description: Bone-in mutton cooked down with tomato, ginger julienne and whole green chilli in a wide copper karahi over a high flame until the fat separates and clings. No onion, no cream. Finished with crushed black pepper at the pass.
menu.seoTitle: Mutton Karahi | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Tomato, ginger and green chilli. Nothing else in the pan.

menu.name: Mutton Shinwari Karahi
menu.shortDescription: Salt, fat and tomato. The Landi Kotal way.
menu.description: The Shinwari style keeps the seasoning to salt and tomato so the meat and its own rendered fat do the work. Cooked longer and slower than the standard karahi.
menu.seoTitle: Mutton Shinwari Karahi | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Salt, fat and tomato. The Landi Kotal way.

menu.name: Mutton Namkeen Tikka
menu.shortDescription: Salt-only tikka, cooked dry in its own fat.
menu.description: Cubes of mutton cooked with nothing but salt and its own fat until the edges crisp. A Pakhtun classic that lets the quality of the meat show or fail.
menu.seoTitle: Mutton Namkeen Tikka | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Salt-only tikka, cooked dry in its own fat.

menu.name: Mutton Dumpukht
menu.shortDescription: Sealed pot, low fire, two hours untouched.
menu.description: Mutton sealed into a heavy pot with yoghurt, browned onion and whole spice, then left over a low fire so the steam never escapes. The lid comes off at the table.
menu.seoTitle: Mutton Dumpukht | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Sealed pot, low fire, two hours untouched.

menu.name: Mutton Roash
menu.shortDescription: Boiled mutton in clear stock, per plate.
menu.description: Mutton simmered gently in clear salted stock until it gives way at a touch, served in its own broth with fresh coriander. Priced per plate on the menu card. The quiet order that regulars swear by.
menu.seoTitle: Mutton Roash | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Boiled mutton in clear stock, per plate.

menu.name: Beef Boneless Karahi
menu.shortDescription: Boneless beef, hard sear, tomato and chilli.
menu.description: Boneless beef cut against the grain and cooked fast in the wide karahi so it never toughens. Tomato, garlic and a great deal of green chilli. Listed by half and full kilo on the menu card.
menu.seoTitle: Beef Boneless Karahi | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Boneless beef, hard sear, tomato and chilli.

menu.name: Beef Qeema Karahi
menu.shortDescription: Minced beef, dry-fried, heavy on ginger.
menu.description: Minced beef dry-fried until every drop of water has gone and only fat and spice remain. Eaten with naan straight from the pan.
menu.seoTitle: Beef Qeema Karahi | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Minced beef, dry-fried, heavy on ginger.

menu.name: Chicken Karahi (Regular)
menu.shortDescription: The house standard. Tomato, ginger, green chilli.
menu.description: Bone-in chicken cooked down in tomato and ginger with a hand of green chilli, finished with coriander. The most-ordered dish in the building.
menu.seoTitle: Chicken Karahi (Regular) | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: The house standard. Tomato, ginger, green chilli.

menu.name: Chicken Namkeen Karahi
menu.shortDescription: No tomato. Salt, pepper and butter only.
menu.description: Chicken cooked in butter with rock salt and crushed black pepper. Pale, rich and completely different from the red karahi beside it.
menu.seoTitle: Chicken Namkeen Karahi | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: No tomato. Salt, pepper and butter only.

menu.name: Chicken Green Karahi
menu.shortDescription: Coriander, mint and green chilli ground to a paste.
menu.description: A fresh green masala of coriander, mint and chilli blended raw and folded through at the end so it keeps its colour and its bite.
menu.seoTitle: Chicken Green Karahi | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Coriander, mint and green chilli ground to a paste.

menu.name: Chicken White Karahi
menu.shortDescription: Cream, cashew and white pepper. Mild by design.
menu.description: Cream and ground cashew carry this one, with white pepper instead of red. The order for a table that includes children.
menu.seoTitle: Chicken White Karahi | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Cream, cashew and white pepper. Mild by design.

menu.name: Chicken Achari Karahi
menu.shortDescription: Pickling spice, mustard oil and a sour finish.
menu.description: Nigella, fennel and mustard seed bloomed in mustard oil give this the sharpness of a mango pickle. Sour, hot and very hard to stop eating.
menu.seoTitle: Chicken Achari Karahi | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Pickling spice, mustard oil and a sour finish.

menu.name: Chicken Full Roast
menu.shortDescription: Whole bird, marinated, roasted, torn at the table.
menu.description: A whole chicken marinated overnight, roasted until the skin lacquers, and brought out whole. Best shared and best with naan.
menu.seoTitle: Chicken Full Roast | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Whole bird, marinated, roasted, torn at the table.

menu.name: Chicken Handi (Regular)
menu.shortDescription: Sealed clay pot, tomato base, finished with cream.
menu.description: Chicken layered into a clay handi with tomato, ginger and yoghurt, sealed and set over a low fire. The cream goes in only at the end so it never splits.
menu.seoTitle: Chicken Handi (Regular) | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Sealed clay pot, tomato base, finished with cream.

menu.name: Chicken Green Handi
menu.shortDescription: The green masala, slow-cooked in clay.
menu.description: Coriander, mint and green chilli paste cooked slowly in a sealed handi. Milder than the green karahi because the long cook rounds the chilli off.
menu.seoTitle: Chicken Green Handi | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: The green masala, slow-cooked in clay.

menu.name: Chicken White Handi
menu.shortDescription: Cashew cream, white pepper, no chilli at all.
menu.description: The mildest thing on the menu and one of the most ordered. Cashew and cream, thickened slowly, seasoned with white pepper only.
menu.seoTitle: Chicken White Handi | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Cashew cream, white pepper, no chilli at all.

menu.name: Chicken Achari Handi
menu.shortDescription: Pickle spice with the patience of a slow cook.
menu.description: The achari masala given forty minutes in a sealed pot instead of ten in a karahi. Deeper, rounder, still sharp.
menu.seoTitle: Chicken Achari Handi | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Pickle spice with the patience of a slow cook.

menu.name: Kabuli Pulao
menu.shortDescription: Mutton stock rice with carrot, raisin and almond.
menu.description: Long-grain rice steamed over mutton stock, crowned with caramelised carrot, black raisin and slivered almond, with pieces of mutton buried underneath. The single dish most often named in reviews, and the one the kitchen is proudest of. Order it a little ahead on a Friday.
menu.seoTitle: Kabuli Pulao | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Mutton stock rice with carrot, raisin and almond.

menu.name: Chicken Pulao
menu.shortDescription: Everyday pulao, chicken stock, whole spice.
menu.description: Rice cooked in chicken stock with whole spice and browned onion. Lighter than the Kabuli and served all day.
menu.seoTitle: Chicken Pulao | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Everyday pulao, chicken stock, whole spice.

menu.name: Mutton Pulao Platter
menu.shortDescription: A tray of pulao under a layer of grilled mutton.
menu.description: Kabuli rice laid out on a wide tray with grilled mutton and salad over the top. Built for four to six and served family-style.
menu.seoTitle: Mutton Pulao Platter | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: A tray of pulao under a layer of grilled mutton.

menu.name: Mix Sabzi
menu.shortDescription: Seasonal vegetables in a light tomato masala.
menu.description: Whatever the morning market gave up, cooked down in tomato and cumin. Cauliflower, carrot, peas and potato most days.
menu.seoTitle: Mix Sabzi | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Seasonal vegetables in a light tomato masala.

menu.name: Daal Mash
menu.shortDescription: White lentil, dry-style, finished with ginger.
menu.description: Urad daal cooked so the grains stay whole and separate, then finished with ginger julienne and a spoon of hot ghee.
menu.seoTitle: Daal Mash | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: White lentil, dry-style, finished with ginger.

menu.name: Chicken Qorma
menu.shortDescription: Browned onion, yoghurt, whole spice. The wedding gravy.
menu.description: Onions browned properly, yoghurt beaten in off the heat, and whole spice left in. The gravy that turns up at every Pakhtun wedding, cooked here every day.
menu.seoTitle: Chicken Qorma | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Browned onion, yoghurt, whole spice. The wedding gravy.

menu.name: Aloo Qeema
menu.shortDescription: Minced beef and potato, cooked down together.
menu.description: Minced beef and diced potato cooked in one pan until the potato takes the fat and the mince goes dark.
menu.seoTitle: Aloo Qeema | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Minced beef and potato, cooked down together.

menu.name: Chicken Fried Rice
menu.shortDescription: Wok rice with egg, spring onion and shredded chicken.
menu.description: Cold rice fired hard in the wok with egg, spring onion and shredded chicken. The order that keeps the younger table happy.
menu.seoTitle: Chicken Fried Rice | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Wok rice with egg, spring onion and shredded chicken.

menu.name: Chicken Chow Mein
menu.shortDescription: Egg noodles, julienne vegetables, chilli garlic.
menu.description: Egg noodles tossed with julienne cabbage, carrot and capsicum in a chilli garlic sauce.
menu.seoTitle: Chicken Chow Mein | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Egg noodles, julienne vegetables, chilli garlic.

menu.name: Tandoori Naan
menu.shortDescription: Pulled and slapped to order. Never sits.
menu.description: Plain naan pulled thin and stuck to the tandoor wall, out in ninety seconds.
menu.seoTitle: Tandoori Naan | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Pulled and slapped to order. Never sits.

menu.name: Roghni Naan
menu.shortDescription: Enriched with milk and ghee, sesame on top.
menu.description: A softer, richer naan brushed with ghee and finished with sesame seed.
menu.seoTitle: Roghni Naan | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Enriched with milk and ghee, sesame on top.

menu.name: Garlic Kulcha
menu.shortDescription: Crushed garlic and coriander pressed into the dough.
menu.description: Kulcha topped with crushed garlic and coriander before it goes on the wall.
menu.seoTitle: Garlic Kulcha | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Crushed garlic and coriander pressed into the dough.

menu.name: House Fruit Sundae
menu.shortDescription: Vanilla, seasonal fruit, jelly and chocolate.
menu.description: The dessert that arrives at every birthday table here. Vanilla ice cream, seasonal fruit, jelly and a chocolate pour.
menu.seoTitle: House Fruit Sundae | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Vanilla, seasonal fruit, jelly and chocolate.

menu.name: Kheer
menu.shortDescription: Rice reduced in milk for three hours, chilled.
menu.description: Rice cooked down slowly in full-fat milk with cardamom, chilled and topped with pistachio.
menu.seoTitle: Kheer | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Rice reduced in milk for three hours, chilled.

menu.name: Kulfa Falooda
menu.shortDescription: Dense milk kulfi over vermicelli and rose syrup.
menu.description: Slow-frozen kulfi set over falooda vermicelli, basil seed and rose syrup.
menu.seoTitle: Kulfa Falooda | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Dense milk kulfi over vermicelli and rose syrup.

menu.name: Sabz Chai (Green Tea)
menu.shortDescription: Cardamom green tea, poured all day, every day.
menu.description: The cup that never stops arriving. Green leaf with green cardamom, poured from height into small cups. Reviewers mention it as often as the food.
menu.seoTitle: Sabz Chai (Green Tea) | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Cardamom green tea, poured all day, every day.

menu.name: Doodh Patti Chai
menu.shortDescription: All milk, no water, boiled down hard.
menu.description: Tea boiled in milk alone until it thickens and darkens. Strong, sweet and heavy.
menu.seoTitle: Doodh Patti Chai | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: All milk, no water, boiled down hard.

menu.name: Salted Lassi
menu.shortDescription: Churned yoghurt, salt, roasted cumin.
menu.description: Yoghurt churned with ice, salt and roasted cumin. What to drink with a hot karahi.
menu.seoTitle: Salted Lassi | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Churned yoghurt, salt, roasted cumin.

menu.name: Fresh Lime Soda
menu.shortDescription: Lime, soda, salt or sugar. Your call.
menu.description: Fresh lime over soda, made sweet or salted to order.
menu.seoTitle: Fresh Lime Soda | Salateen Restaurant Swabi
menu.seoDescription: Lime, soda, salt or sugar. Your call.

menu.description: A cold 1.5 litre bottle, whichever brand the cooler is holding.

menu.seoDescription: Chilled bottle for the table.

chefs.name: Gulzar Ahmad
chefs.title: Head Chef
chefs.bio: Gulzar started on the tandoor in Mardan at fourteen and has run the Salateen kitchen since the restaurant opened. He still checks every degh of Kabuli Pulao himself before it leaves the pass, and he will tell you, at length, that the secret is the stock and nothing else.
chefs.quote: Rice does not forgive a weak stock. Everything else you can fix.

chefs.name: Fazal Rabi
chefs.title: Grill Master
chefs.bio: Fazal runs the charcoal pits. Fourteen years of turning skewers by hand have given him a sense for the coals that no thermometer replaces. He lights the fire at four every afternoon and does not leave it until closing.
chefs.quote: Good coals are grey, not red. Red coals burn the outside and leave the middle raw.

chefs.name: Hidayat Ullah
chefs.title: Karahi Chef
chefs.bio: Hidayat handles the copper pans. On a Friday evening he will run six karahis at once across two burners without writing anything down.
chefs.quote: A karahi is finished when the oil comes up clear. Not a minute before.

chefs.name: Shakeel Ahmad
chefs.title: Tandoor Baker
chefs.bio: Shakeel has been at the tandoor for nine years. Naan leaves his hands and reaches the table in under two minutes, which is the only standard he accepts.
chefs.quote: Bread that waits on the counter is bread you should not have made.

testimonials.name: Asad Khan
testimonials.title: The full platter genuinely feeds ten
testimonials.quote: We were a party of eleven for my brother’s graduation and one platter plus a tray of pulao was more than enough. Bill came to about six thousand. I have not found value like this anywhere between Swabi and Peshawar.

testimonials.name: Rabia Noor
testimonials.title: The Kabuli Pulao is worth the drive
testimonials.quote: We come from Mardan roughly once a month purely for the Kabuli Pulao. The rice is never sticky and the mutton underneath is always tender. The green tea keeps arriving without asking.

testimonials.name: Imran Shah
testimonials.title: Chapli kabab like Peshawar
testimonials.quote: Proper coarse mince, proper anardana, fried in beef fat the way it should be. Service slowed down a little at peak time but the food made up for it.

testimonials.name: Hina Gul
testimonials.title: Family hall was perfect for us
testimonials.quote: Booked the family hall for a walima reception of about thirty. Full purdah, clean, and the staff were respectful throughout. The manager arranged everything over the phone.

testimonials.name: Kamran Khattak
testimonials.title: Best BBQ on this road
testimonials.quote: The seekh kabab and the mutton chops are the reason I stop here on every trip to Swabi. Chops were slightly dry once but they replaced them without an argument.

testimonials.name: Sana Ullah
testimonials.title: Quail roast was a surprise
testimonials.quote: Ordered the batair roast on the waiter’s recommendation and it was the best thing on the table. Also try the fish fry in winter.

testimonials.name: Zubair Marwat
testimonials.title: Delivery arrived hot
testimonials.quote: Ordered a full chicken karahi and naan to Mal Lar. Arrived in under thirty minutes and still steaming. Free delivery because the order was over 2,500.

testimonials.name: Farah Naz
testimonials.title: Kids loved the white handi
testimonials.quote: The white handi has no chilli at all, which made it the only thing my children would eat. Big portions and the sundae for dessert made it a good evening.

testimonials.name: Tariq Mehmood
testimonials.title: Shinwari karahi done properly
testimonials.quote: Salt, tomato and fat, nothing else. That is how it should be and that is how they make it. The lawn seating beside the grill pits is worth asking for.

testimonials.name: Naveed Anwar
testimonials.title: Reliable for large groups
testimonials.quote: We book here for office lunches every couple of months. Never had a problem getting a table for twenty with a day’s notice.

testimonials.name: Maria Khan
testimonials.title: Green tea and chapli in the afternoon
testimonials.quote: The chai and chapli deal in the afternoon is my regular. Rs 220 and it is a proper meal.

testimonials.name: Waqar Zeb
testimonials.title: Catering for our mehndi
testimonials.quote: They catered our mehndi for a hundred and forty guests. Deghs arrived on time, hot, and the servers stayed until the end. Everyone asked where the pulao came from.

blogs.title: What Makes a Real Kabuli Pulao
blogs.excerpt: Everyone claims it. Very few earn it. Our head chef on stock, rice and the twenty minutes that decide everything.
blogs.body:
Ask ten cooks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa how to make Kabuli Pulao and you will get ten answers. Ask Gulzar Ahmad, who has run this kitchen since 2011, and you get one: it is the stock, and everything else is detail.

## The stock is the dish

We start the yakhni before the restaurant opens. Mutton on the bone, whole black cardamom, a little cumin, and enough water to cover. It sits at a bare simmer for close to three hours. Nothing is added to make it darker or richer, because anything you add to compensate is a confession that the stock was thin.

A weak stock gives you rice that tastes of water and spice. You can add more spice. It will not help. The grain has already decided what it is going to taste like.

## Rice that stays separate

We use super kernel basmati and we soak it for forty minutes, no longer. Over-soaked rice breaks in the pot and gives you a pulao that eats like a biryani that lost its nerve.

The rice goes into the boiling stock and comes out at seventy percent. That number matters. It finishes in the steam, not in the liquid.

## Carrot, raisin, almond

- Carrot is cut into matchsticks and caramelised separately in ghee with a pinch of sugar. It goes on at the end so it keeps its edge.
- Black raisin is plumped in warm stock, never water.
- Almond is slivered the same morning. Yesterday's almond tastes of the tin.

## Twenty minutes of dum

The pot is sealed and set over the lowest flame we can manage for twenty minutes. Nobody opens it. Nobody stirs it. This is the part every home cook rushes and it is the part that separates a good pulao from the one people drive in from Mardan for.

When the lid comes off, every grain should stand apart, and the mutton underneath should give way to a spoon. That is the whole test.

blogs.title: The Charcoal Question: Why We Have Never Moved to Gas
blogs.excerpt: Gas is cleaner, cheaper and easier. We still light hardwood every afternoon at four. Here is why.
blogs.body:
Every year somebody suggests we convert the grill pits to gas. The arguments are always good ones. Gas is cheaper. It is cleaner. It does not need a man standing beside it from four in the afternoon until midnight.

We have not done it, and we are not going to.

## What charcoal actually does

A gas flame heats by convection. Hot air moves across the meat and cooks it from the outside in. Charcoal heats mostly by radiation, and radiant heat behaves differently: it drives into the surface fast, sets a crust in seconds, and leaves the interior alone long enough to stay wet.

That crust is where the flavour lives. On a seekh kabab it is the difference between a piece of grilled mince and something worth ordering twice.

## Grey coals, not red

Fazal Rabi, who runs our pits, has one rule he repeats to every new hand: wait for the grey.

Red coals are still burning off volatiles. They flare, they smoke sourly, and they scorch the outside before the middle has warmed. Grey coals are past that stage and give a steady radiant heat you can actually work with.

This is why we light at four for a service that starts at seven.

## The part nobody sees

Charcoal is inconsistent. Every sack is a little different. A gas burner set to a number is the same on Monday and Friday; a coal bed is not. The only way to work with it is to have somebody who reads it by eye and by the back of their hand.

That person is the reason we can serve four hundred skewers on a Friday night without a single one going out dry. No thermostat replaces them.

blogs.title: How to Order for a Party of Twenty
blogs.excerpt: A practical guide to feeding a large table at Salateen without over-ordering or leaving anyone short.
blogs.body:
We seat large tables every day and the same two mistakes come up. People either order one dish per person, which leaves half of it uneaten, or they order too conservatively and end up adding at the end when the kitchen is at its busiest.

Here is what actually works.

## The rule of thumb

For twenty adults, budget roughly:

- Two Grand Platters (serves 10 each), or
- One Grand Platter plus a full tray of Kabuli Pulao and two full karahis

Add three to four kilos of BBQ across seekh, tikka and chops. Add twenty-five to thirty naan. Add two portions of daal mash and one mix sabzi for anyone who wants a break from meat.

## Order the pulao first

Kabuli Pulao takes thirty-five minutes and a full tray takes longer. If you tell us the pulao when you sit down rather than when the BBQ arrives, everything reaches the table together.

## What to ask for

- A corner of the main hall or the family hall. Both take twenty comfortably.
- One karahi mild if children are eating. The white karahi or white handi has no chilli at all.
- Raita and salad per six people, not per person.

## What not to over-order

Naan. Every table over-orders naan. Order twenty and add more if you need them; they take ninety seconds.

## Give us a call

For twenty or more, a phone call on 0312-0991116 an hour ahead means the deghs are already on when you arrive. It costs nothing and it saves you forty minutes.

blogs.title: Chapli Kabab: A Short History of a Flat Kabab
blogs.excerpt: Why the Peshawari kabab is flat, why it contains pomegranate seed, and what most versions get wrong.
blogs.body:
The name comes from *chaprikh*, the Pashto word for flat. That is the whole explanation, and it is also the first thing most recipes outside the region get wrong: a chapli kabab that is thick is not a chapli kabab.

## Why flat

Flatness is not decoration. A wide, thin disc gives you the maximum ratio of crust to interior, which is the entire point of a kabab shallow-fried rather than grilled. Thicken it and you get a patty that steams in its own moisture.

## The pomegranate seed

Dried pomegranate seed, *anardana*, does two things. It provides acid, which the beef needs, and it provides small pockets of moisture that burst during frying. Lemon juice cannot replace it. Vinegar certainly cannot.

## Coarse, not fine

The mince must be coarse. Fine mince binds into a paste and eats like a sausage. We grind ours on the widest plate and we do not overwork it. If the mix looks like it will fall apart, it is about right.

## The fat matters

We fry in beef fat. This is not nostalgia. The fat carries flavour back into the kabab as it cooks and gives the crust a texture that oil does not.

## The tomato slice

The tomato slice pressed into the top is not garnish either. It protects the surface as it fries and steams the top of the kabab while the bottom crusts. Remove it and you get an even kabab, which sounds better and eats worse.

blogs.title: Why the Green Tea Never Stops Arriving
blogs.excerpt: Sabz chai costs fifteen rupees and we lose money on almost every cup. We are not going to change that.
blogs.body:
Our menu card lists sabz chai at fifteen rupees. It has been at that price for a long time and, at current leaf and gas costs, we make almost nothing on it and often less than nothing.

We are asked about this fairly often, usually by people who mean it kindly.

## Melmastia

In Pashtun custom, hospitality is not a service you sell. *Melmastia* is an obligation on the host, extended without expectation of return and without regard to who the guest is. Charging a guest properly for tea would be, in a small but real way, a failure of that.

So the tea keeps coming. Nobody counts the cups.

## What we actually sell

The economics work because tea is not the product. The karahi is the product. The pulao is the product. The tea is the reason a family stays for two hours instead of forty minutes, and the reason they come back in three weeks.

If you want to reduce it to arithmetic, it is the best marketing spend in the building. But that is not really why we do it.

## How it is made

Green leaf, green cardamom, sugar to taste, poured from height so it aerates on the way into the cup. The pouring is not showmanship; it cools the tea to drinking temperature and lifts the cardamom.

Ask for it without sugar and we will bring it without sugar. Ask for a second pot and we will bring that too.

blogs.body:
When we planned the building in 2011, the family hall was the first room we drew. In Swabi it is not an amenity, it is the difference between a restaurant a family can use and one they cannot.

## How it is arranged

The hall holds eight tables behind full-height partitions, each screened so that no table is visible from another or from the corridor. Service is by a dedicated attendant who announces before entering. Tables seat from six to twelve.

## Who it is for

Families, obviously. But also:

- Women dining without male relatives
- Small walima and mehndi receptions of up to forty
- Anybody who simply wants a quiet table

There is no minimum spend and no surcharge.

## Booking it

Individual tables can be booked through the reservation page or by phone. For the whole hall, call 0312-0991116 at least three days ahead. We will hold it without a deposit for parties under forty.

## What to ask for

Tell us the occasion when you book. Birthdays get a cake stand and the house sundae on the house, and we will keep the lighting up or down as you prefer.

blogs.title: Where Our Mutton Comes From
blogs.excerpt: One supplier, six years, and a standing rule that nothing frozen enters this kitchen.
blogs.body:
We buy mutton from one house in Swabi and we have done for six years. It costs us more than shopping around and we have no intention of changing it.

## The rule

Nothing frozen. Everything arrives in the morning and is used the same day or the next. Anything not used by the end of the second service is not sold; it goes to staff meal or it goes out.

This is why we occasionally run out of the mutton dishes late on a Friday. We would rather tell you it is finished than serve you something that has sat.

## Why one supplier

A single relationship means the butcher knows exactly what we need and how we break it down. Chops come at a consistent thickness. Karahi cuts come bone-in at the right size. Roash meat comes from the right part of the animal.

You do not get that from whoever is cheapest this week.

## What we check

Every delivery is weighed and inspected on arrival, logged against the purchase order, and entered into the stock system before it goes into the cold room. If a batch is not right it goes back the same morning.

Boring, and completely necessary.

blogs.title: Winter Is River Fish Season
blogs.excerpt: From November the karahi over the wood fire is mostly fish. Here is why you should order it.
blogs.body:
From late November until roughly March, the open karahi outside the kitchen door is mostly fish, and that is the time to order it.

## Why winter

River fish in this region is at its best in the cold months. The flesh is firmer, the fat content is higher, and it holds together in the batter instead of falling apart in the pan.

## How we do it

Whole fish, scored to the bone so the heat gets in, coated in a spiced gram-flour batter with ajwain and red chilli, and lowered into the wide karahi over a hardwood fire.

The wide pan matters. A deep fryer at a set temperature gives you an even, dull result. An open karahi over wood has hot and cool zones, and a cook who knows how to move the fish between them gets a crust that no fryer produces.

## How to eat it

With naan, lemon, and raw onion. Not with rice. Ask for the chutney.

## A note on bones

It is river fish. It has bones. We score it and we serve it whole because that is how it tastes best, and we would rather warn you than fillet it into something lesser.

blogs.title: What Catering a Walima Actually Involves
blogs.excerpt: Deghs, timings, staffing and the three decisions that matter most.
blogs.body:
We cater between eight and fifteen functions a month in Swabi district, most of them walimas and mehndis. The ones that go smoothly all get the same three things right.

## One: decide the count early

Everything scales off the guest count and everything has a lead time. A hundred and forty guests means roughly:

- Six deghs of Kabuli Pulao
- Four deghs of mutton karahi
- Twelve kilos of chapli kabab
- Six kilos of mixed BBQ
- Four hundred naan, baked on site

Tell us seven days ahead and none of this is difficult. Tell us the day before and some of it is impossible.

## Two: decide the serving time, then subtract

Pulao holds well for about ninety minutes in a covered degh. BBQ holds for twenty. If your serving time slips, the pulao is fine and the BBQ is not.

We build the schedule backwards from the time you tell us, so the accuracy of that time matters more than anything else on the order.

## Three: decide who is serving

Above two hundred guests we send our own service staff and chafing dishes as part of the package. Below that, most families use their own. Either works, but decide it early, because it changes how the food is packed and delivered.

## What we need from you

A confirmed count seven days out, a venue address with a phone number for someone who will actually be there, and fifty percent in advance. Everything else is our problem.

blogs.title: How to Tell if a Karahi Is Finished
blogs.excerpt: One visual cue tells you everything. Most kitchens serve five minutes before it appears.
blogs.body:
There is exactly one reliable test for a finished karahi and it is visual: the oil comes up clear and separates at the edge of the pan.

## What the separation means

While there is water left in the tomato and the meat, the fat stays emulsified into the sauce and the whole thing looks uniform and slightly dull. As the water cooks off, the emulsion breaks and the fat rises, clear and glossy, and pools at the edges.

That break is the moment the dish changes from stewed to fried. It is where karahi flavour comes from.

## Why most kitchens miss it

Because it happens late, and because the dish looks perfectly acceptable five minutes earlier. Under pressure, an acceptable-looking karahi goes to the pass.

We hold ours. This is occasionally why your karahi takes thirty-two minutes and not twenty-five.

## What you should look for

When it arrives, tilt the pan slightly. If a clear rim of oil runs at the edge and the masala clings to the meat rather than pooling under it, it is right.

If the sauce is thin and the oil is mixed through, it went out early. Send it back. Any kitchen worth eating in will take it.

faq.question: Do you deliver, and where?
faq.answer: Yes. We deliver across Swabi city, Mal Lar, the Jhangira Road corridor, Yar Hussain, Topi, Kalu Khan, Panjpir, Zaida, Marghuz and Shewa Adda. Delivery charges range from Rs 60 to Rs 200 by area, and delivery is free anywhere inside Swabi city on orders above Rs 2,500.

faq.question: What payment methods do you accept?
faq.answer: Cash only. For delivery orders you pay the rider in cash when the food arrives. For dine-in you pay at the counter. We do not currently accept cards or online payment, and we never ask for payment details online.

faq.question: Is there a minimum order for delivery?
faq.answer: Yes, and it varies by area, from Rs 1,500 in Mal Lar up to Rs 3,200 for the furthest zones. The minimum for your address is shown at checkout as soon as you pick a delivery area.

faq.question: How long does delivery take?
faq.answer: Between twenty and fifty-five minutes depending on your area and how busy the kitchen is. The estimate shown at checkout is the one we work to. On Friday evenings, add fifteen minutes.

faq.question: Can I order the Grand Platter for delivery?
faq.answer: Yes, though we recommend calling 0312-0991116 forty minutes ahead. It is a large tray and it travels best when it goes out the moment it is finished.

faq.question: What is your most popular dish?
faq.answer: Kabuli Pulao, without much competition. After that, the Chapli Kabab, the Chicken Karahi and the Beef Seekh Kabab.

faq.question: Do you have vegetarian options?
faq.answer: Yes. Mix Sabzi and Daal Mash are fully vegetarian, and the breads, salads, raita, desserts and drinks are as well. Everything is cooked in a shared kitchen, so please tell us if you need it kept strictly separate.

faq.question: Is all your food halal?
faq.answer: Yes, everything we serve is halal without exception. Meat comes from a single Swabi supplier we have worked with for six years.

faq.question: Do you have anything mild enough for children?
faq.answer: Yes. Chicken White Karahi and Chicken White Handi contain no chilli at all. Chicken Pulao and Chicken Fried Rice are also mild, and the kitchen will make almost anything without green chilli if you ask.

faq.question: How does half-kilo and full-kilo pricing work?
faq.answer: Most karahis, handis and kababs are priced by weight of the cooked dish, exactly as on our printed menu card. A half kilo comfortably serves two, a full kilo serves four alongside rice and bread.

faq.question: Do I need to book a table?
faq.answer: Not on a weekday. On Friday and Saturday evenings, and for any group over eight, we strongly recommend it. Booking is free and takes a minute on the reservation page.

faq.question: Can I book the family hall?
faq.answer: Yes. Individual family-hall tables can be booked online. For the whole hall, which takes up to forty, call 0312-0991116 at least three days ahead.

faq.question: How far ahead can I book?
faq.answer: Up to sixty days. Bookings need at least two hours notice so the kitchen and floor can plan.

faq.question: What happens after I submit a reservation?
faq.answer: It arrives as pending and the manager confirms it, usually within an hour during opening times. You will see the status on the reservation confirmation page and in your account.

faq.question: Is there a charge to cancel?
faq.answer: No. Cancel any time from your account or by phone. We only ask that you tell us, so the table can go to someone else.

faq.question: What are your opening hours?
faq.answer: Ten in the morning until midnight, every day of the year including Eid.

faq.question: Is there parking?
faq.answer: Yes, free of charge. There is a parking lot for around thirty cars plus free street parking on Jhangira Road.

faq.question: Is the restaurant accessible?
faq.answer: Yes. The entrance, the main hall seating, the toilets and the car park are all wheelchair accessible. Tell us when booking and we will hold a table with easy access.

faq.question: Do you have outdoor seating?
faq.answer: Yes, on the lawn beside the grill pits, plus marquee seating in winter. Ask for the outdoor zone when you book.

faq.question: Do you cater weddings and functions?
faq.answer: Yes, from a hundred guests upwards, anywhere in Swabi district. We supply deghs, and above two hundred guests we send serving staff and chafing dishes as part of the package. Book at least seven days ahead with fifty percent in advance.

faq.question: Can you cook a whole goat or lamb?
faq.answer: Yes, with three days notice. We take the order, source the animal and cook it whole, and this is a common request for functions.

faq.question: Do you have a kids menu?
faq.answer: Yes, and children are genuinely welcome. High chairs are available on request.

faq.question: Can I get a receipt or invoice for a company lunch?
faq.answer: Yes. Ask at the counter and the cashier will print one with your company name on it.

faq.question: Are you hiring?
faq.answer: Usually. Current openings are listed on the careers page, and you can always drop a CV at the counter.

events.title: Friday Charcoal Night
events.description: Every Friday from seven, the pits run at full capacity and the whole BBQ section is served family style on shared trays. Live tandoor, unlimited sabz chai and the lawn open until midnight.

events.title: Eid Family Buffet
events.description: Three days of Eid, three services a day. Kabuli Pulao, mutton karahi, chapli kabab, BBQ, four salans and dessert, laid out in the family hall and the main hall.

events.title: Winter River Fish Festival
events.description: Four weeks from mid-December, the open karahi runs fish all evening. Whole river fish fried to order, with naan, chutney and raw onion.

events.title: Graduation Season Platters
events.description: Through July and August we hold the family hall for graduation parties. Grand Platter pricing for groups, cake stand and photographs arranged on request.

events.title: Chef's Table: Kabuli Pulao
events.description: Twelve seats around the pass while Gulzar Ahmad builds a degh of Kabuli Pulao from the stock up. Two hours, tasting throughout, questions encouraged.
highlights: Two hours with the head chef

events.title: Ramadan Iftar Service
events.description: Iftar laid out across all three halls throughout Ramadan, with dates, fruit chaat, pakora, the full menu after Maghrib and sehri service until 4am.

cateringPackages.name: Majlis
cateringPackages.description: Our entry package for family functions and small receptions. Kabuli Pulao, one karahi, chapli kabab, salad, raita and naan, delivered hot in covered deghs.

cateringPackages.name: Shahi
cateringPackages.description: Two rice dishes, two karahis, full BBQ selection, two salans and dessert. Serving staff included above 200 guests.

cateringPackages.name: Salateen Royale
cateringPackages.description: The full kitchen at your venue. Whole roast goat, three rice dishes, four karahis, the entire BBQ section, four salans, three desserts and a live tandoor.
includes: Live tandoor and live BBQ station

cateringPackages.name: Corporate Lunch
cateringPackages.description: Individually packed lunches or a shared buffet for offices and institutions, delivered at a fixed time every day or on a schedule.

cateringPackages.name: Aqiqa & Small Functions
cateringPackages.description: A compact package for aqiqas, birthdays and small gatherings, either at your home or in our family hall.
includes: Family hall option at no extra cost

jobs.title: Grill Chef (Charcoal Section)
jobs.description: Work the charcoal pits alongside our grill master. Responsible for marination, coal management and every skewer that leaves the section.
responsibilities: Prepare and manage the coal bed from 16:00
Marinate and portion BBQ items to spec
Turn and finish all skewers to order
Maintain section hygiene and close down the pits
requirements: Minimum 3 years on a charcoal grill
Able to work evening and late shifts
Understands marination timing for beef, chicken and mutton

jobs.title: Tandoor Baker
jobs.description: Run the tandoor through service. Naan, roghni and kulcha, pulled to order and out in under two minutes.
responsibilities: Prepare and prove dough daily
Bake to order through service
Maintain tandoor temperature and cleanliness

jobs.title: Floor Supervisor
jobs.description: Run the floor across the main hall, family hall and lawn. Manage the waiter team, reservations and guest recovery.
responsibilities: Manage seating and reservations through service
Supervise and roster the waiting team
Handle guest complaints on the spot
Coordinate with the kitchen pass
requirements: 3+ years hospitality experience, at least 1 supervising
Fluent Pashto and Urdu, working English

jobs.title: Delivery Rider
jobs.salaryRange: Rs 32,000 per month plus fuel and tips
jobs.description: Deliver across Swabi city and the surrounding zones. Own motorcycle preferred, fuel allowance provided.
responsibilities: Deliver orders within the estimated time
Collect cash and reconcile at end of shift
Keep the delivery box clean and food safe

jobs.title: Cashier & Accounts Assistant
jobs.description: Handle the counter, daily reconciliation and supplier payments.
responsibilities: Operate the counter through service
Reconcile cash daily against the system
Process supplier invoices and payments
Maintain purchase records
requirements: Comfortable with spreadsheets and POS software

jobs.title: Kitchen Porter
jobs.description: Support the kitchen with prep, washing and stock movement. Training provided, and a genuine route into a chef role.
responsibilities: Wash and maintain kitchen equipment
Basic vegetable and meat prep
Move stock between store and kitchen
requirements: Physically able for a busy kitchen
